Image 1 is the scene. Keep it exactly as it is — same camera, same framing, same television, shelf and brackets, same cable, same shelf of binders and taped sketches, same paper and palette.

Image 2 is a layout guide for what goes ON the television screen only. Ignore its red lines, its black arrow and its caption entirely; use only the arrangement of boxes inside the screen.

Change ONE thing: the television's dark screen is now lit and pale, and on it is a drawing of a cluttered online shop's product page, laid out as image 2 arranges it: a menu bar across the top; a wide advertising banner beneath it; a big framed picture of a paper shopping bag at the left; beside the picture the product's title, its price, and a stack of boxes and buttons; a row of four small related-item pictures beneath; a thin scrollbar down the right edge; and a wide cookie-notice bar across the bottom of the screen with its own small button. Every word of text on the page is drawn as this film draws text: rows of small graphite dashes and short blocks, zero letters. The one important detail: the shop's real buy button is TINY — a small, thin-lined, pale grey box tucked into the bottom right corner of the page, half hidden behind the cookie bar, easy to miss. Draw no cursor and no arrow anywhere.

Draw the whole page in graphite line in the same hand as the rest of the picture, the way a pencil-test animator would draw a web page — hand-ruled boxes, slightly wobbly lines, cross-hatch on the picture, a faint pale wash on the banner and the buttons. It is a picture on the television.

Hand-drawn animation pencil test: graphite line, visible construction lines, cross-hatch shadow, light coloured-pencil wash on props only, paper tooth showing — no flat vector fill, no digital gradients, no painterly rendering, no photographic lighting, no 3D. Do not add any legible text or letters anywhere in the picture.
